From Taino/Arawakan 'iwana', first recorded in Richard Eden's 1555 'Decades of the New World' where he described creatures resembling crocodiles measuring eight feet long — one of the earliest written records of any indigenous Caribbean word entering European languages.

From Taino/Arawakan 'mahiz', borrowed into Cuban Spanish and then English in the 1550s; Europeans called it 'Turkey corn' for centuries under the mistaken belief that it came from Turkey, the same geographic confusion that gave turkeys their name.

From Narragansett or Abenaki Algonquian 'moos' or 'moz', meaning 'he strips off' — a reference to the moose's habit of stripping bark from trees in winter; the animal's name is literally a description of its feeding behavior, not its appearance.

From Tupi 'pira nya' — 'pira' (fish) + 'nya' (biting), literally 'biting fish'; the name entered English via Portuguese in 1869, and the Tupi-speaking peoples of Brazil gave the world's most feared freshwater fish one of the most literal names in any language.

From Quechua 'cuntur', the sacred native name for the world's largest flying bird; the Inca venerated the condor as a messenger to the gods and carved it into ritual objects — the bird entered English around 1600 along with Spanish accounts of the Inca empire.

From Quechua 'puma', the Inca word for the mountain lion that was a central symbol of Inca military power — the Inca capital Cusco was reportedly designed in the shape of a puma from above; the word entered English in 1777 via Spanish colonial accounts.

From Nahuatl 'mizquitl', the Aztec name for this shrub of the pea family; first recorded in English in 1759 via Mexican Spanish, the tree was so critical to desert survival that many Southwestern American place names are derived from it — the Nahuatl root outlasted the Aztec empire by centuries.

From Powhatan/Algonquian 'makasin' (shoe), documented in the 1610s; by 1784 the same word had been applied to venomous snakes in the American South — etymologists remain baffled by the sense connection between footwear and a deadly snake, calling it 'difficult to explain'.

The ornamental garden flower is named after tobacco: French botanists coined 'petunia' (1789) from 'petun', their word for the tobacco plant, which came from Guarani 'pety'; the petunia was recognized as a botanical relative of tobacco, and its name still carries that connection.

An argosy — a large merchant ship laden with treasure — is not named after the mythical Argo but after Ragusa, the Adriatic city-state now known as Dubrovnik, Croatia. In the 1570s, Ragusan merchant vessels ('nave Ragusea' in Italian) dominated trade between the Levant and England; the city's name garbled into 'argosy' as its ships became synonymous with wealth.

The soft, napped leather is named after Sweden — via a French fashion trend. In the 1850s, French glove-makers marketed butter-soft kid-skin gloves as 'gants de Suède' (gloves of Sweden); the material's name entered English in 1884, though the Swedish gloves that inspired it were long forgotten.

The word 'cognac' is simply the name of Cognac, a small town in the Charente region of western France. References to 'Conniacke wine' appear as early as the 1590s; by the 1680s it specifically meant the double-distilled brandy that had made the town famous — a direct, unbroken line from French terroir to English vocabulary.

Cologne (the fragrance) is named after Cologne, Germany — where Italian chemist Johann Maria Farina created his signature scent in 1709, naming it 'Eau de Cologne' (water from Cologne). The city itself had been 'Colonia Agrippina' since 50 CE, named for Agrippina the Younger, wife of the Roman emperor Claudius, who was born there.

The archaic English word for shoemaker — 'cordwainer' — survives from medieval Córdoba, Spain, the city whose tanneries produced the finest leather in Europe. Workers who crafted shoes from that Cordovan leather became 'cordwainers'; the Guild of Cordwainers in London, founded in 1272, still exists today under that name.

From Sanskrit pandita, a title for scholars rigorously trained in Vedic texts, law, and sacred language — a credential requiring decades of study. By 1816, English was using it loosely for any opinionated commentator, a dilution that would horrify the original panditas.

This everyday nursery word comes from Hindi khat and Sanskrit khatva, meaning a couch or hammock. British sailors adopted it in the 1760s for canvas hammock beds on ships, and it eventually settled into English as the folding child's bed we know today.

This small boat word traces back to Hindi dingi, from Sanskrit drona-m meaning 'wooden trough' — itself from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning firm, solid wood. The same ancient root that gave us 'tree,' 'durable,' and even 'Druid' also gave us the humble dinghy.

Named after Calicut (modern Kozhikode) on India's Malabar Coast — a Tamil trading port so famous for its white cotton exports in the 1530s that the fabric took the city's name. By 1807 Americans were using 'calico' to describe any multi-patched animal coat, from horses to cats.

From Hindi bandhan, 'the act of binding,' itself from Sanskrit badhnati, 'he binds.' A bandana is literally a binding cloth — and remarkably, it shares a deep Proto-Indo-European ancestor with the English word 'bind,' making them linguistic twins separated by thousands of years.

Sanskrit upala simply meant 'gem' or 'precious stone' — no specific color or type. The word traveled through Greek opallios and Latin opalus before reaching English in the 1590s, retaining the same meaning across three millennia of trade routes and language change.

Sanskrit khanda meant 'piece of sugar' — a word for the chunks of crystallized cane sugar traded across the ancient world. It traveled through Persian qand and Arabic qandi into French before reaching English in the 13th century, meaning specifically crystallized sugar for centuries before broadening to all confections.

Sanskrit srngaveram meant 'horn body' — a vivid description of the knobby shape of a ginger root. The word passed through Prakrit, Greek, Latin, and Old French before reaching Old English, making ginger one of the oldest Sanskrit-origin words in the language.

Sanskrit pippali referred specifically to long pepper, a distinct plant that was the main spice of ancient trade. When Spanish explorers found hot chili plants in the Americas in the 1500s, they named them 'pepper' after the unrelated Asian spice — and the mistaken name stuck for all capsicum plants worldwide.

Tamil mankay combines man ('mango tree') and kay ('fruit') — a straightforward compound that traveled through Malay and Portuguese before English traders documented it in the 1580s. The same Captain Bligh infamous for the Bounty mutiny introduced mango trees to Jamaica in 1793.

Sanskrit mantra literally means 'instrument of thought' — from man ('to think') and the tool suffix -tra. It entered English in 1808 referring to Vedic hymns; today it is used for everything from meditation phrases to corporate mission statements, drifting far from its sacred origins.

Sanskrit yoga means 'union' or 'yoking' — specifically the union of the individual soul with the universal spirit through meditation. The same Proto-Indo-European root gave English 'yoke' and 'join.' Today's billion-dollar fitness industry has made yoga almost entirely about physical postures, stripping the original metaphysical core.

From Hindi dungri, the name of a village near Bombay (now Mumbai) where coarse blue cotton cloth was produced. The fabric entered English records in the 1610s as sailors' workwear; by 1868, 'dungarees' had shifted meaning entirely — from a cloth type to the trousers sewn from it.

Danish botanist Wilhelm Johannsen coined gene in 1909 by clipping the last syllable of pangene (a term coined by Hugo de Vries), itself from Greek genea 'generation, descent.' He simultaneously invented the terms genotype and phenotype to describe the difference between genetic code and observable traits.

From Greek klon, 'twig or cutting from a plant.' The word began as a pure botany term — American plant physiologist Herbert Webber introduced it in 1903 to describe plants propagated from cuttings. Only in 1963 did J.B.S. Haldane extend it to the sci-fi sense of genetically identical beings.

Antoine Lavoisier coined the word in 1777 from Greek oxys ('sharp, sour') and -genes ('born of') — literally 'acid producer,' because he believed, incorrectly, that oxygen was the essential ingredient in every acid. The name enshrined a scientific error that we still use today.

From Old French bescuit, from Medieval Latin biscoctum: bis ('twice') + coctus ('cooked'). Medieval bakers literally baked bread twice — once to cook it, once to dry it out completely — creating the rock-hard, non-perishable ration carried by Roman legions and medieval sailors.

From Portuguese marmelada, a preserve made from marmelo ('quince'), which traces back through Latin to Greek melimēlon — literally 'honey apple.' English records show marmalade imports as early as 1480; for its first 150 years in English it meant a quince preserve, not citrus.

Named for Paisley, a town in west Scotland whose weavers began copying Kashmir shawls on jacquard looms after 1800. The motif itself — called boteh or buta in Persian — is 2,500 years old, but 'paisley' as the English name stuck because Scotland became the dominant European manufacturer.

Despite its Celtic associations, tartan likely comes from French tiretaine, a coarse linsey-woolsey cloth (attested in French from the 13th century), not from Scottish Gaelic. The clan-specific pattern system so beloved today was only invented around 1815 — historians now consider it a largely fabricated tradition.

From Greek gymnasion, from gymnazein 'to exercise naked' — because gymnos meant 'naked.' Greek athletes truly competed and trained nude, rubbing themselves with olive oil. The word carried that literal meaning into Latin and then English before politely dropping the nudity connotation.

Named in 1803 by English chemist Smithson Tennant from Greek Iris, goddess of the rainbow, because the element's salts dissolved into a dazzling array of colours — reds, yellows, blues — unlike anything previously seen in a single metal. The element's name is literally 'rainbow metal.'
'Meat' in Old English meant any food at all — vegetables, dairy, and grain were all 'meat.' The meaning narrowed over centuries until it referred exclusively to animal flesh.

'Deer' was the Old English word for any wild animal at all — bears, wolves, and boars were all 'deer.' It narrowed to one specific creature, probably because deer became the most prized quarry of hunters.
'Cute' started as a shortening of 'acute' in the 1730s, meaning clever, sharp-witted, and shrewd. By the 1830s American slang had converted it entirely into a word for physical attractiveness.
'Pretty' originally meant 'cunning, crafty, and wily' — describing someone skilled in tricks and deception. Today it is purely about physical appearance and attractiveness.
'Quick' originally meant 'alive, living' — the phrase 'the quick and the dead' survives to remind us. Today the word exclusively means fast or rapid, with its life-and-death origins forgotten.
A 'spinster' was simply a woman whose occupation was spinning thread — a neutral job title. It morphed into a legal and then derogatory term for an unmarried older woman.

A 'pedant' in the 1580s was simply a schoolmaster or teacher — a neutral occupational title. Within a decade it had flipped to mean someone who flaunts minor knowledge in an irritating, narrow-minded way.
Around 1300, 'girl' referred to any child or young person regardless of sex — a boy could be a 'girl.' It narrowed to female only by the late 14th century.
'Brave' traces to roots meaning 'wild, savage' and possibly even 'cutthroat or villain' in Medieval Latin. It elevated over time into the admirable quality of courageous valor we celebrate today.

From Arabic 'laimun' and Persian 'limun', possibly tracing back to Malay 'limaw' — Arab traders brought the fruit and its name from India to the Levant in the 9th or 10th century, from where it spread across the Mediterranean into European kitchens and languages.

From Persian 'karwan' — a group of desert travellers — the word entered European languages through the Crusades and was reinforced by Silk Road traders; what started as a term for camel-borne merchant convoys eventually became the British word for a holiday trailer.

The glass vessel on restaurant tables comes from Arabic 'gharrafa' — a vessel for drawing water, from 'gharafa' meaning to draw or scoop — travelling through Italian and French before becoming standard English table vocabulary in 1786.
